utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kriste, I listened to your testimony carefully yesterday during the examination-in-chief, and I should like to ask you several things. I'd like your explanations to the Trial Chamber about something you might still not have said about the negotiations you had in Split and everything else that you did in and around Dubrovnik. You were given assignments from the government as to what your duties were in Split and Dubrovnik, what you had to accomplish there; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were given tasks for Dubrovnik. As for Split, we stayed there for just one day, waiting to receive permission to enter Dubrovnik. And at the request of the president of the Crisis Staff and the Executive Council of the Municipal Assembly, we took part with them in the talks and negotiations with General Mladenic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And as you said yesterday, you were working on an agreement that you had concluded, and I'm interested in one aspect of that and that is the deblocking of the barracks in Split. You took part in those negotiations, did you not? So under what conditions was the barracks in Split deblocked? You said that that was the substance of your negotiations.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the negotiations were to discuss the departure of the Yugoslav navy from the Lora port on the one hand and also, on the other, the return of the weapons of the Territorial Defence to the town of Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you more directly: You know that on the 21st of August, 1991, Vladimir Seks informed the public that the barracks' electricity, water, and food supplies would be cut off. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. And at the end of August, did this actually begin in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some cases the barracks were blocked, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that on the 25th of August the barracks were blocked in Split? Are you aware of that? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that particular piece of information.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Tapuskovic. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In response to a question from the Prosecution yesterday, you answered that a certain agreement had been reached and what your demands were of the JNA. And an agreement was reached; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And was the response, as you said previously in your statement to the investigators, that in return for that, Croatia should cease its blockade of the barracks in Split? Was that one of the points of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, that was not how it was formulated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That is what it says in your statement to the investigators, and I'm quoting it verbatim: "In return, Croatia was to put a cessation to the blockade of the JNA barracks in Split."

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, we did discuss the blockade of the Lora port.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Which is where the JNA soldiers were; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So that means that the blockade lasted --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The microphone seems to be switching off of its own accord.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If the blockade was set up at the end of August, that means that it lasted for almost three months.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know when the blockade started, but even if it did go on until or, rather, from the end of August to the 20th of September, that would not make it three months; end of August, end of September. The fact is that towards the end of August, before we arrived in Split, what happened was that there was an offensive on the part of the Yugoslav navy from the Brac channel targeting Split, and probably a blockade of the port by the Yugoslav Navy was probably linked to the attack launched on Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let's just clear one more point up. You said the 29th of September, but in your statement it says that the agreement was concluded on the 2nd of December.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's a mistake. That's a mistake -- or, rather, yes, you're quite right, the 2nd of December. I'm awfully sorry. Yes, it was on the 2nd of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what I was interested in. Now, something I'm much more interested in and a point that I'd like to assist the Trial Chamber on is the following, for them to be able to understand the situation around Dubrovnik: Was your task when you went off together with two other ministers, and those ministers were Cifric and Rudolf - both of them were ministers in the government of Croatia, just like yourself - was your task and assignment, among other things, this: To do all you could to ensure a cease-fire in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was our task in the Dubrovnik region to conclude a cease-fire, a truce, yes, in addition to other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And of course, stopping the shooting.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. A truce includes a cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about that because it says in your statement "cease-fire," but I suppose "truce" is the same thing. So when you arrived there, you said you talked to Nojko Marinovic, who was a general. Was he the commander of the defence of the town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to him before the negotiations that took place on the 5th of September and afterwards as well, and did he attend the negotiations with you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We talked to him before and after the negotiations but he did not attend the negotiations with us. He wasn't there with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I should like now to indicate to you something that I consider should be done today. A rare witness which we have according to Article 66 of the Statute because the Prosecutor has put him forward as a witness but he has not been questioned yet, but he has been proposed also under Article -- Rule 68, and that man is Nojko Marinovic. I have a copy of his statement, several copies to go around, and Mr. Kriste talked to the commander. I should like to tell him some things from the statement and everything that happened in those few days in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can put the statement to the witness. It's not appropriate at this stage to have it admitted. Maybe in due course we'll consider it. But if there's something you want to put from that statement to the witness, you can do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In the talks, either before or after, did Mr. Nojko say that as you were going to attend the negotiations, did he give you this piece of information to inform you by way of information, and I'm going to tell you exactly what he said. He says in his statement the following: "Our strategy was essentially to gain time. Because of that, we always wanted to reach an agreement on a cease-fire, and this was for two reasons: First, to gain time; and second, not to waste our valuable resources. But most essential point was also that during the cease-fire and truce, we had a much better chance of bringing in, smuggling in through the maritime route both equipment and personnel." Is that what Nojko Marinovic told you when you met him?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it would be proper to put to the witness the reference, the context in which Mr. Marinovic mentioned these kind of considerations, because there was a long time of negotiations ongoing in which the witness was not included, and it should be made clear whether these references were related to these earlier negotiations in October and in November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We need to be careful about this. We are going some way from the point of what the witness has said. Mr. Kriste, if you can help with this, what counsel is reading out to you, if you can help, say so, but if you know nothing about it and it is something which the general is dealing with himself, then simply say so and we'll get on more quickly. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic, let's go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not receiving the interpretation, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's try again. Is it right? Now, try again. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you now. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What I'm saying is this: We may be going some way from evidence on which you can help us anyway, because these may be matters that you know nothing about, but if there is something you can help us about, tell us. If not, and it was something which the general was dealing with and you know nothing about, then simply say that you know nothing about it and we can get on more quickly. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic. Let's deal, if we can, with matters the witness might know about. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we are not challenging the fact that Nojko Marinovic was the commander of the defence of Dubrovnik. Mr. Kriste came to negotiate a cease-fire, a truce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We know that. Now, let's move on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Does Mr. Kriste know that a strategy of that kind existed, namely to gain time, and in the meantime they were doing their best to arm the people?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not our strategy. Our strategy was to achieve a lasting truce and peace ultimately, a truce and cease-fire of the hostilities and the establishment of a truce.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: For a time you were the war minister. Do you know what Mr. Tudjman said on the 24th of May, 1992, at a large rally that took place on Ban Jelacic square? Did he say precisely what Nojko said, because he said that is why we waged a policy of negotiation, and behind these negotiations, we established armed units. Is that what he said?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember what Mr. Tudjman said exactly in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As you attended the negotiations, this is what I'd like to say to you, and I'm reading from Nojko's statement. He said how many people there were as defenders of the town, and on page -- I'll give you the page straight away of Nojko's statement and read it out to you. Did Nojko, before you went to attend the negotiations or afterwards, perhaps, say on the first day of the attack, 1st of October, 1991, "the Croatian forces under my command numbered the following," and then he said, "670 soldiers." Is that what he said?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 1st of October, when we were in Dubrovnik, he set out the whole situation, the military situation in Dubrovnik. He told us what the enemy forces were, what their strength was and deployment. And he also told us that our forces were completely unready both numerically, that they were in an inferior position for them to be able to put up an effective resistance to the JNA forces. And he mentioned some facts and figures; the number of policemen and also the number of members of the Croatian National Guard Corps, which was somewhere around 100 or 200 men. And he also told us that there were a large number of citizens, citizens of Dubrovnik who had responded as volunteers to take up the defence but that there was not enough weapons to go around.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kriste, I'm just asking you - and give me a yes or no answer - did he say that there were 670 soldiers under his command? Did he tell you that or not?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not mention that particular figure, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And did he say that they had been deployed from Slano on the west to Ban, which is one kilometre from the Montenegrin border towards the east, and that they covered a distance around the road of about 75 kilometres? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not give us the specifics and go into details as to the deployment of our forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And did he say that four guns, cannons, 85-millimetre guns that they had seized from Korcula, that they were deployed two above Cavtat and two at Rasnica near Molunat? Did he tell you that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't say where they had been deployed, where the guns had been deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did he say you that two zis anti-tank guns were set up in Babin Kuk in Dubrovnik and the other near the Neptun Hotel, once again in Dubrovnik? Did he tell you that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that he did not give us the specifics of the deployment of men and forces on our side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And did he say ten anti-aircraft guns?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has answered this. He said he was not given the specifics. So, Mr. Tapuskovic, there is no point putting any more detail to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, Judge May, I really think -- I don't know whether Mr. Nojko Marinovic will come to court, but Nojko Marinovic did state that they had cars and trucks with anti-aircraft guns positioned on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- you've put all that, and the witness has told you what his answer was. Now, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That he doesn't know. Now, Your Honours, please. I think that you should be interested in all of this material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This, for example --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- there is a limit of time, as you know, which we can put up -- which we can allow for any examination. Now, the accused has had over two hours with this witness, and we must ask you now - you've had nearly 20 minutes - to come to an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall do my best and get through the essential points. As the witness said that on the day he arrived in Dubrovnik, before the 1st of October, that he had brought in a truck of mines and explosive devices with his colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is that correct, Witness?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mines and explosive devices, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know that Nojko Marinovic stated that all that -- those explosive devices deployed from Montenegro to Dubrovnik along the road, that holes had been dug and mines placed in them, that this existed at intervals of 100 metres, one hole with a mine and then the next one without a mine and so on?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't tell me that, but with a truckload of this kind, you won't have enough mines to mine such a large number of kilometres along a road. Apart from that -- with a truck trailer load. But if Mr. Marinovic did carry out this mining of the area, this was on the territory of Croatia and on the territory of the Dubrovnik municipality, and nobody could have fallen casualty to that unless he had launched a war operation against Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as I really don't have any more time, I'm going to conclude with this question: You said that the positions of the JNA army was not targeted at all from Dubrovnik, from Dubrovnik proper, from the town itself. That's right, isn't it? That's what you said?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, not from Dubrovnik. We could not open fire from Dubrovnik and target the JNA units until the JNA army had not closed off the encirclement around Dubrovnik and came right close up to Dubrovnik. I said yesterday that the free territory of Dubrovnik stretched for about ten or 12 kilometres, and at that point in time, the weapons that we received were placed in this free stretch of land. But I underlined in particular that this was not in the old town itself nor near the old town. That's what I emphasised.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You know that Mount Srdj is an area which is above the ramparts, above the city walls, above the town.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And the fighting was predominantly around Mount Srdj?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around Mount Srdj, and the town was shot at too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, let me say -- tell you what Nojko said about the 6th of December attack. "All the guns -- practically all the guns that we had, and did you see that on that day, all the cannons that I had in Dubrovnik were directed towards Mount Srdj. In fact, the first 48 shells with which we opened fire were very valuable, so we had to use them well. The artillery did not have any scope. If we were allowed -- if I had allowed the shelling, we would shell three grenades and then the artillery would have to receive further permission to continue fire." Now, this kind of firing and shooting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us stick with what this witness can answer. He was merely a spectator, his evidence has been, of the attack, the shelling of the town. Now, are you disputing, Mr. Tapuskovic, that the town was shelled?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not disputing that the town was shelled, Your Honour Judge May. All I'm asking is did he see that shooting was coming from the town, as Nojko Marinovic describes it? Did he see shells being fired from Dubrovnik at Mount Srdj? I've been to Dubrovnik many times and stood on the terrace of Hotel Argentina and you can see the old part of town.

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was on the terrace of the Argentina Hotel and I did not see any targeting and shooting towards Srdj because, from the Argentina Hotel, you can see the area of the old town and its surrounding ramparts and parts. The area of Lapad, for example, the other side, and other areas that were still under our control but further away from the old city walls, you could not see and control from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you just answer me this, please: Where is the Lero Hotel situated in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hotel Lero is Gospin Polje, which is about three kilometres away from the town walls.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you can't see it from --

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You can't see even if there's shooting coming from the hotel?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kriste, just to start with the last question that you were just asked, Mount Srdj, how many -- how much above is it of the old town? What is the distance between the old town and Mount Srdj, the fort on Mount Srdj?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Srdj is just above the old town. I wouldn't be able to tell you exactly what the altitude is, but the old town is at the foot of Mount Srdj.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kriste, Mr. Milosevic, in his cross-examination, put to you that you were a close associate of Mr. Tudjman, and my question is: In the period relevant here - that is 1991, 1992, 1993, 1994 - were you a close associate of Tudjman? Were you close to him?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that period, I was not a close associate of Mr. Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic put to you that Mr. Tudjman's aspiration in -- were actually Croatia up to the Drina River. When did he have these ideas, and did he give this up at some point in time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This idea that according to historical logic and in view of the composition of the population of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it would be logical for Bosnia and Herzegovina to be part of Croatia, this is a thought he uttered at the beginning of December 1989 in a conversation I had with him. He gave up that idea and never for a moment was anything specific done on the part of Croatia to implement that idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic cited in his cross-examination from the newspaper interview, and he referred to your talks with Susak, and I would like to clarify something. Did you have two conversations with Susak at different times?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The first conversation with Mr. Susak, when did it take place and what did he actually tell you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first conversation took place late in March or the beginning of April 1991. That was just after our media had published the report that in a border location Mr. Milosevic had met with Mr. Tudjman. In that conversation, all he said to me was that he was coming from the old man, meaning the leader. In answer to my question why he seemed so happy, he said he was coming from the old man and that the decision had been taken or agreement had been reached that Herzegovina should be annexed to Croatia. I -- that was when the conversation ended. We just met and parted.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you met him and he made this remark, did he in any way refer to taking this territory by force?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you relate this remark to the negotiations that you had read about and heard about, the negotiations between Milosevic and Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the Croatian government in 1991 make any moves towards annexing this part of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This other conversation with Mr. Susak, when did it take place and what was the context?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in October 1992. We met at the Split airport. In those days, according to media reports, it was possible to conclude that there Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. would be an aggravation of Croato-Muslim relations. And I asked him whether it was possible to do anything to ease those tensions. His response was what I have already stated, that is, that --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that a unit was on the move from Prozor and that there would be no prisoners taken. And I understood this to mean a true escalation of poor, bad relations between the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims. I mean the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic referred in his cross-examination to actions of General Bobetko. Those actions, were they related in any way to the attack on Dubrovnik in 1991 or what was going on in Dubrovnik in 1991?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The two had nothing to do with one another. It was not connected to what was happening in 1991 because Bobetko went to the southern front in the 5th -- in May or June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you say "southern front," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the Dubrovnik area.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic put to you that the JNA in Croatia had actually two goals. The first was to protect those endangered, regardless of their ethnicity; and secondly, to protect its own units that were blockaded all over Croatia. Would you agree that this is -- these were the goals?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I do not agree that those were the goals of the JNA. The JNA was actually acting as the military force of the Republic of Serbia, and it was operating in Croatia with the aim of achieving the goals of that policy. In fact, the Yugoslav People's Army, and especially after the war in Slovenia, ceased to be that in the real sense of the word. True, it retained the name of the Yugoslav People's Army, but it was already becoming a Serbian army because it had been deserted by young conscripts of all ethnicities, with the exception of Serbs, but also some young men from Serbia. At least, in Croatia there were some Serb conscripts who were deserting the army and demanding to be allowed to go home in Serbia. Similarly, the command staff, that is the officers of the Yugoslav People's Army who were not of Serbian ethnicity, after that war and partially also before that, either left the army of their own free will or were removed from responsible positions, so that the period we're talking about, that is the autumn of 1991, the Yugoslav People's Army, which was still called that, was in fact operating as a Serbian military force. Anyway, the army ended up by being transformed into three armies, and that is --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: If I can interrupt you. You have already described this. What I wanted to know: Did the army protect the people regardless of their ethnicity, the JNA?

utterances.speaker: PETAR KRISTE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army did not protect the people regardless of their ethnicity. The army was always on the side of the Serbs, and columns consisting of all non-Serbs fled before the onslaught of the army as it gained control over various areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kriste, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to raise one issue in closed session in relation to the witness that will follow the next one. Not Mr. Simunovic but C-013.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I trust the Chamber has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to say for the record that while I was sick in bed, I received another 40.000 pages from the opposing side. I would just like this to be recorded, that I pointed out at the end of the summer and before the beginning of this second part that I had 115.000 pages received during the Kosovo trial for Bosnia and Croatia, that I asked for time, and that you gave me, for 115.000 pages and the opening statement, two weeks, considering this to be sufficient. Now the figure has gone up to over 300.000 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not going to argue about this now. You had, as you knew, a considerably longer period between the two parts. But we're not going to discuss it now. Let's hear the witness's evidence, and then if you've got any applications about new material, we'll certainly hear them in due course. We will allow time for it. But let's hear the witness now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, Mr. Milosevic. We're going to get on with the evidence and then we'll come back to these procedural matters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you haven't answered my objection having to do with receiving the documents in my own language. I am given statements by Serbs, Muslims in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll come to this. We'll come to this, but now we've got a witness. Let's hear his evidence. He's waiting. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, Mr. Milosevic. Unless you've got an application about this particular witness, we're going to hear his evidence. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we'll hear your application later in the morning. Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is your full name Ivo Simunovic; were you born in April 1950; you are a Croat; you went through school and college in Dubrovnik; you did national service between 1974 and 1975, continuing thereafter as a reserve officer, completing reserve service in 1982?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were a businessman in Dubrovnik for some 16 years, between 1975 and the outbreak of war in 1991. And in August of 1991, you joined the local Croatian Territorial Defence, being one of a limited number of reserve officers available for service with the Croatian defence forces in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Could I please receive the Croatian interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Simunovic does in fact speak good English, but obviously his evidence must be given in --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. It's fine now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Picking up on the last point, the Croatian Territorial Defence you joined in August 1991, to what extent did it have weapons? What type of weapons, if any?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: The Croatian defence had little weapons in 1991. It is well known that the weapons of the Territorial Defence of Dubrovnik were stored in Duzi, a village in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, so that we couldn't get hold of those weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you have any heavy weapons? Did you have sidearms?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: In those days, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Dealing with the social situation in Dubrovnik generally and very briefly, did the Serb population of Dubrovnik constitute about 6 per cent of the total?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there any history of ethnic tension in the Dubrovnik area? If not, what was the relations like between Croats and Serbs generally?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: There were no ethnic tensions whatsoever. Relations were good.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As things deteriorated in Croatia, so far as you could judge, was there an expectation that Dubrovnik would be involved or an expectation that it would be an exception and not be involved?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: At first we thought that it would bypass us and that we wouldn't be involved. However, as things developed in the republics of the former state, we soon realised that we -- our turn would come very soon too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What, if any, was the defining event or the turning point in the expectation of people in Dubrovnik as to what would happen to them?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Primarily the events around Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As a result of those events, did people in Dubrovnik take steps to defend themselves?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: The population of Dubrovnik at the time didn't do anything. However, the Ministry of Internal Affairs did take certain steps at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you one of those who got involved?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: I joined on the 22nd of August, through the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A few words about military background and the general military position in 1991. You've told us that Territorial Defence weapons were stored elsewhere. Did that follow demilitarisation of the town or the old town in 1969 when the old town became a UNESCO protected site?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: The protected -- the old town was proclaimed a monument of culture as opposed to the rest of Dubrovnik, which was not part of this heritage and protection area, protected area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was it at this time that the weapons you've spoken about went to Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were there any JNA facilities in the old town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Before the aggression, no. And during the aggression, there weren't any either, if you mean units of the Croatian army. There were no units of the Croatian army in the protected part of the old town of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were there any such units in the wider area of Dubrovnik before the aggression started?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: There were only on the part of the so-called Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As of late August or September 1991, were there different groups involved with defence of the region, including the Croatian National Guard, the Territorial Defence, and the police?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The National Guards were part of the Ministry of the Interior, units of the special police and the Territorial Defence which later joined to come under a single command and became the so-called armed forces of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Continuing with the position before they combined, at that early stage, what sort of number of men were involved in the various groups and what sort of weapons were available to them?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, there were about 200 soldiers, and all they had were so-called long-barrel personal weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In your judgement, how efficient and organised was the National Guard at this early stage?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: If you're referring to the National Guards Corps, they were a small unit in the process of formation. They didn't have any experience, not even military experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And your judgement on the Territorial Defence, of which you were a part, as to its preparedness to fight and so on.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence was better prepared due to the very fact that officers joined who had all been reserve officers in the former army, so we had some knowledge which we were able to put to use for the defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Had there been, again in August, early September of 1991, had anything been done to establish defensive positions to take care for any JNA offensive?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: In those days, since it was within the competence of the police administration of the Dubrovnik-Neretva region, they built some obstacles along certain routes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Anything beyond that?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At roughly the same time but probably a bit earlier, had a Crisis Staff been formed in Dubrovnik to deal with civilian issues?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So far as you're aware, did that have any military component to it or not?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's turn, please, to General Marinovic. Who was he? What role did he take? What did he do, in summary?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: General Marinovic joined the Croatian army, or the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia, on the 17th of September, 1991. He came from Trebinje, and in Trebinje, he had been commander of the JNA garrison; a Croat by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did he do? What did he achieve in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: His first assignment upon coming to Dubrovnik was to unite all these small forces to form a single unit under his own command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was he successful in doing that?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Very successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was the overall strategy that he and those of you working with him formed?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: The strategy in those days consisted exclusively of how to defend ourselves, how to defend Dubrovnik, that is the territory of the former municipality of Dubrovnik, which stretched from Montenegro to Ston.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what was judged to be the best method of defending yourselves against attack?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: We had good assessments, but we didn't have the necessary resources to be able to act according to our assessments. And I primarily mean that we lacked weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To what extent did delay play any part in the strategy that you formulated?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: It had a major impact, because we had tried to prepare ourselves for what we knew would happen already in mid-September. That is, an attack on our municipality. And our strategy was to try and prepare ourselves as well as possible for that and to arm ourselves as well as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Between September 1991 and December 1991, can you approximate the number of men involved in defending Dubrovnik and its region.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Roughly 300, not counting the regular police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was that a figure that fluctuated or was it stable?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: The number fluctuated downwards and upwards with time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did that number of men constitute an equal match for what the JNA had available or not?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't an equal match.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What degree was there inequality?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: In the types of weapons and in the numerical strength.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there any intention - paragraph 14 - to defensively against the JNA at any time?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: There were no such intentions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Dealing with the old town, what, if any, was the policy as to the storage or use of weapons on or from the old town?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: If you are referring to the protected part of the town of Dubrovnik, there were absolutely no possibilities. And also, the order was that soldiers or units could not be present in the protected old town of Dubrovnik, as opposed to other parts of Dubrovnik where we functioned normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before the first attack on Dubrovnik, can you give us, please, an estimate of what weaponry was available to you, what weaponry you'd been able to obtain, if any, from elsewhere. Did you have any heavy weaponry before these attacks?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: In the second half of September, we managed to procure from the island of Korcula three guns, 96-millimetre calibre, which had been left behind by the Yugoslav People's Army when they withdrew from that island. However, those guns had no sights and covers which meant that they were almost useless. And these were the only heavy weapons that we had in Dubrovnik prior to the 1st of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Light weaponry, what was available?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: In limited quantities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's turn to the night of the 30th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I produce through the witness another map, part of your Exhibit 326. May it become tab 14. The Chamber will have seen this area before, but for convenience we can look at it on this particular map. It shows an area south of Dubrovnik including the Bay of Kotor and the Prevlaka peninsula.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 30th of September, where were you by reference to this map? What did you see, please?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: On the 30th of September and earlier too --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the microphone be switched on, please, the other microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 30th of the September and prior to that date, I was in the area of Vitaljina, that is the Prevlaka peninsula between Molunat and the Ostropina at Prevlaka. A couple of days earlier, I had also toured our positions in Vitaljina, and I went to look and see what was going on there. And I noticed -- but I must point out that all the days prior to the 30th, fire was opened on us from these heights on the side of the Republic of Montenegro. That is where the Yugoslav army was positioned. But luckily, we were not hit. But I must say that on the 26th, 27th, 28th, and 29th, battleships were shelling this area of Vitaljina. But what I do wish to underline was that the 30th, the Yugoslav Army, from these heights on the Montenegrin side of the border, used light bullets to shell the area of the Prevlaka that were being captured by the JNA. Of course, they were not hitting them, but looking at the map, it is to the left. How can I judge? Because they were using these light bullets, and it was easy to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I realise there's a problem with the microphone, but if you could please use the pointer and just without commentary because of the microphone problem point out on the map where you were, roughly.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where the JNA was firing from.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And where it was firing to. What was it hitting?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that's the area just off the peninsula to the north. Thank you very much. But before that, there had also been shelling from the sea and onto Croatian territory from --

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: There were, from patrol boats. Molunat, starting from the 26th and on the 27th and on the 29th.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Tracer bullets, not light bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we look at the next exhibit, which will become 336, 15. Sorry. 336 IS. Beg your pardon. This is a copy from our atlas which the witness has marked in preparation to save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In summary, please, Mr. Simunovic, using this map -- if we can get a microphone that works so he can use the overhead projector, so much the better but if it doesn't, it doesn't. In a good loud voice - perhaps the microphone will pick you up - could you explain, please, what happened on the 1st of October.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: I'll begin regardless of the fact that I'm not receiving any interpretation. On the 1st of October, from several directions, there was an attack on the former municipality of Dubrovnik from the access of the Prevlaka area at the Talina [phoen] and from the direction of Sutorina, towards Debeli Brijeg, and from the direction of the town to the village of Dubravci. From the direction of the town, as I said, towards the village of Dubravci, and from the Trebinje direction towards the hills of Konavle, and from the Trebinje area towards Brgat, as well as from Hum, which is the Trebinjsko Polje area, towards Osojnik. And then we have another axis, the direction towards Ston and Slano, from Orahovo down there towards Slano. And that was also the axis towards Cepikuce that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. happened the next day, because on the first day of the attack, the 1st of October --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... to some degree you've used terms that are slightly different from those on the legend of the map. The seven lines shown on the map, 1 to 7, do those indicate the lines of attack that you've been telling us about?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: We also have another line of attack from the sea and a line of attack from the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They haven't been translated; those are numbers 8 and 9 on the legend.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Nine, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Simunovic. So involved in this attack was the army, navy, and the air force. Before we move on, one matter that I ought to have dealt with about the night of the 30th of September: The firing of the JNA, was it all onto Croatian territory or was there any firing of the JNA onto what was itself a JNA position?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: The JNA, at the time, was located on Croatian territory, and the Prevlaka peninsula is part of Croatian territory. However, that's where there was a unit of the Yugoslav People's Army, a JNA position.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was that fired on by the JNA from elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: No. It did not respond to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there firing onto that JNA unit on Croatian territory?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: If you mean from the positions in Vitaljina which were held by the Croatian policemen, no, it was not fired at.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's move back to the 1st of October and to the attack you summarised on the map. What were the Croatian defence forces able to do in response to this attack?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: As what was happening was happening, the Croatian forces did try to prevent it, to prevent the breakthrough and advance of the Yugoslav People's Army along these lines, these axes. The composition of the Yugoslav army, which was advancing along these nine lines of attack towards the former Dubrovnik municipality, was as follows: We had fighting against us, the Hercegovina Corps. Then there was the Podgorina Battalion, Podgora Battalion, the Valjevo Battalion, the battalion from Radovici, the guns from Danilovgrad, the tank battalion, the air force - and the planes were coming from Podgorica and Mostar - the navy from the navy military district, and then there was a helicopter unit from Danilovgrad. And when you see this whole composition, it numbered between 6.000 and 8.000 men, soldiers. When you look at the strength of it all, the strength that they used to deploy in the area and attack the area, it is frightening. However, at that time, we weren't that frightened. We didn't allow ourselves to be frightened. So they advanced very slowly, disproportionately to the amount of strength and manpower that they had at their disposal, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And could you, by reference to the map, show to what degree you were forced back from the areas you previously held or areas you previously occupied.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: From the direction of the Vitaljina Prevlaka, the forces of the Yugoslav People's Army, in the space of three days, arrived to join up with the forces of Sutorina Gruda, those that moved from Sutorina towards and advanced on Gruda. The village of Ban in this eastern area of Konavle fell or, rather, was burnt down and looted on the 3rd. That means three days, it took three days for that army to take control of these 20-odd kilometres. And they drew three front lines moving towards the Dubrovnik airport, which was rocketed first on the 6th and only on the 10th were the military forces able to enter. Cilipi, the airport, and Cilipi were also burnt down, and reached Dubrovnik. On the 15th, the forces of the Yugoslav People's Army reached Cavtat, so it took them a full 15 days to unite, to conjoin with the other axes from Herzegovina in order to reach Cavtat on the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pausing there. In the course of that, was one enemy tank destroyed in Konavle? If so, how?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was, by a hand -- by a mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. So far as the attack from the north was concerned, what success did that have? What success did you have in slowing it down?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Twenty-four days the forces needed from Trebinje to take control of the village of Brgat above Dubrovnik. They needed a full 24 days. And they took control of it when they descended upon Kupari and when the units of the Trebinje Corps joined up with the Hercegovina Corps and the units that were moving from the sea. Only at that point did Brgat fall.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the course of this attack or these attacks, did the JNA limit its attack to military targets or were civilians, in your experience and judgement, ever involved?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: In that part, the fewest soldiers were killed. We were in charge of protecting that company of ours, but outside all military regulations, the civilians were killed, their houses were looted and burnt. Let me also mention that along this line of attack, the Yugoslav air force took part in it as well as the navy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As a result of the attack, did civilians seek refuge in the old town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: The civilians or part of the civilians from Konavle were put up in the Croatcia Hotel, and part of them fled and took refuge in the town of Dubrovnik proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we now have another map, Exhibit 326, to become tab 13? It's slightly -- it's already in evidence. Thank you very much. It may not be the strongest picture, but if the Chamber would like to have an A3-size map, I think they've got that. It shows a number of features that are perhaps important to know just a little about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you point out, please, to us so we all know where it is, the old town just so that we're sure what we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: It is a protected area. The old town of Dubrovnik is located here. That's the circle. And Dubrovnik starts with Belvedere and ends right over here. So this whole area is considered to be the area of the town of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can see Rijeka Dubrovacka running in from the sea. That becomes significant later north of Dubrovnik. Immediately north of Dubrovnik we can see a little oblong box marked "Srdj." Can you just tell us about that, please. S-r-d [sic] on the map.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: This is a fortification.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And we're going to see a --

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: This is the fortress, the fortification in which the television communications and links were --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: -- set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll see a fleeting picture of this in a video a little later, but as the map shows, it's high above the town, and I think it's an ancient fortification. Over to the north or north -- north-west of that, there's a place called Strincera. Tell us about that, please.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Strincera. That is the next fortification up on the Srdj plateau.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. There's one other site that we may want but it's off the map, so we'll come to that in the course of the narrative. Tell us, please, in summary, about the attack and events on the 23rd of October.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: On the 23rd of October, the units of the Yugoslav army joined up from the Trebinje direction and Konavle, and looking at that date, that was the first open attack on the town of Dubrovnik. But we forgot to say that when the attack on Dubrovnik was launched on the 1st of October, that the planes targeting the Srdj -- Mount Srdj and destroyed the transformer station and TV lines so that Dubrovnik had neither electricity or water as of the 3rd of October. By linking up -- to go back to what we were saying, by linking up the troops, the attack was launched on Mount Srdj. That is to say an attack on civilian targets in the town of Dubrovnik itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you expecting an attack on the old town or were you surprised by it?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: We were not expecting it. May I have the interpretation, please? We were not expecting an attack on this protected area as a cultural monument in the old part of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And on the 23rd and through to the 24th, what sort of targets were focused on by the JNA? Did they include civilian targets? If so, which?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: In most cases, they were exclusively civilian targets. And in what I said earlier on, I said that we didn't have many military units, so that they were deployed over a broad area. We had to space them out. And they were targeted, they were shot -- civilian facilities, houses, settlements were shot at and targeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What about the harbour and its boats? What about the hospital?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: The hospital was also targeted, regardless of the fact that it was displaying the International Red Cross emblem. This happened, and unfortunately, there was a direct television broadcast over Bosnia-Herzegovina television showing the army from Osojnik targeting civilian facilities in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Boats; and if they were in a harbour, where was the harbour? Point it out for us, please.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout the duration of the aggression against Dubrovnik, the ships of the Yugoslav People's Army were attacking the town itself, Lapad and this area here, the Lapad peninsula. And they launched their attack with the ammunition, fragmentation bullets, and guns were also used and mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By the 1st of November, where had the JNA reached in its attack?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: By the 1st of November, it had reached the positions here. That is to say, the villages behind Dubrovnik were emptied of the inhabitants, and they reached Petrovo Selo and Osojnik. It is even more northerly than you can see on the map. That was on the 1st of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is there an area called Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, it's not on this map, but it should be to the right of the village of Bosanska, another two kilometres from there. And they took control of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And does Zarkovica have high ground? If so, how high, with what view over the old town?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Zarkovica, in fact, dominates part of the town of Dubrovnik. And from Zarkovica, you can't see just a portion of the Gruz harbour. And it is at an altitude of about 300 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you say you can't see a portion of the Gruz harbour, do you mean you can see everything else except a portion of the Gruz harbour?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the Chamber will see that Gruz harbour is the limb of the water immediately north-west of the town, coming off the Rijeka Dubrovacka. You can see Luka Gruz mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the highway, did they reach a place called Dubac?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And that's where they stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think we may have mentioned already Mokosica on the Rijeka Dubrovacka. Just point that out for us again.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: It is a housing settlement in the Dubrovacka Rijeka; Stara and Nova Mokosica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And from this point on, was Dubrovnik, as you've shown us really by what you've pointed out, effectively surrounded?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, from that point onwards, Dubrovnik was surrounded as far as the town of Dubrovnik itself is concerned. However, Dubrovnik was cut across when the place called Slano was taken control of. Our communications were cut off. And with the advent of November, Dubrovnik was actually under siege, surrounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did the JNA have all the high ground except the one point that you've already told us about, Mount Srdj?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Yugoslav army held under its control everything but Srdj; Sinjova [phoen] and Zarkovica and the village of Osojnik to the north-west of Gruz harbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll see Mount Srdj remained untaken for a combination of reasons and a bit of good luck. Tell us what happened between the 10th and 13th of November, please, in a couple of sentences.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: On the 10th and 13th of November, there was an attack on Dubrovnik, of Mount Srdj and the entire Dubrovnik area, and the Yugoslav army, this was one ever its attempt to enter Dubrovnik. They were prevented from doing so and we know the outcome of the previous one. They did not succeed in their intention to take control of Srdj hill, Mount Srdj and the fortress at Srdj, but we had serious civilian casualties during that attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. We've moved to November and detailed some particular attacks, but had negotiations for the cease-fire, or a cease-fire, started as early as the 18th of October, and were you a member of the negotiating team acting in that capacity on the orders of General Marinovic?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: I joined on the 18th of October, joined in the negotiations as a representative of the Croatian army on the negotiating team composed of Mr. Nikola Obuljen and Mr. Djuro Kolic. We discussed -- we tried in a certain way to gain time and to show the international community what was going on, because the international community was always present at the meetings. We tried to show them what the situation was like around Dubrovnik, and we tried to explain to the other side, that is to say the Yugoslav army, what they were doing there, and who were they defending us from, defending us from themselves and that they had no place there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there were many meetings. In order to save time but to enable the witness to be asked questions on detail, if it's appropriate and anybody wants to, we have reduced the summary of negotiations into a chart. May I produce that, please. One for the witness, please. May it be given an exhibit number? Mr. Simunovic -- may this have an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Prosecutor's Exhibit number 371, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Simunovic, does this chart which you have had prepared or has been prepared from information you've provided reflect in summary form the dates, locations, and composition of cease-fire meetings?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You can see that they were on an almost daily basis, to begin with all in Cavtat, later in other locations including Cavtat. In the course of these meetings - and I want to deal with most of this in very general terms - did you make complaints about the shelling of the old town?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: The first point on the agenda of our negotiations and at every meeting was military matters, and in it we presented everything that had to do with the actions taken by the Yugoslav army against civilian targets in the Dubrovnik town area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What, if there was a general response, was the general response of the JNA to that?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: The meetings would usually evolve in the same way; they would refute it, and they would also threaten us at those same meetings. And at one particular meeting, they said that if we shot one single shell, they would retaliate with tens of shells against the town of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What, if any, excuse did they give for shelling the old town?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, quite simply, at that time they gave us no excuse or explanation. They explained this away by saying that there were a large number of military facilities deployed in our town, so that after this same meeting, both we and them would have a good laugh.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is there any truth in their suggestion that there were such units deployed in the old town?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the Croatian units were, of course, in the Croatian town of Dubrovnik. However, nobody gives anybody the right to target civilian targets and facilities. The military facilities that were targeted, we didn't discuss those. All we wanted to discuss and stop was the killing of civilians and targeting of civilians in the Dubrovnik area and further afield in the surrounding parts too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, one more question out of paragraph 26, seeing the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Apart from these meetings, did you have the ability to contact the JNA directly during attacks? Did you contact them? If so, with what request and what was their response?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were able to contact them directly. We had a direct line, direct communications through the maritime radio and also through the phone, telephone connections. And we would contact them, and I talked to quite a number of senior officials and officers when the attacks took place, but the attack would not cease until, I assumed, the target they had in mind was hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what -- we're talking about your making these contacts and making complaints. Of what were you complaining in particular?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: We were complaining about the artillery fire targeting civilian targets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is a convenient time. We will adjourn now. Mr. Simunovic, we're going to adjourn for 20 minutes. In this adjournment and any others there may be during your evidence, would you remember not to speak to anybody about it until it's over, and that does include members of the prosecuting team.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we must take some time this morning to deal with the application made by the accused about some extra material being served on him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm getting the detail of that provided, and I'll be in a position to deal with it sometime in the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Simunovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 27, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Simunovic, in your face-to-face or telephone contacts with the JNA negotiators or other officers, did they ever complain about inability to communicate with those in the field or up their chain of command?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: The Yugoslav army had a chain of command which meant that nothing could happen by chance or outside that chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did these particular officers ever allege to you that they were having any difficulties with the standard methods of communication with which you were familiar?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: In the official part of our meetings, no. But after the meetings or before the meetings, the atmosphere was quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did they say then?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: That we had to understand them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did your radio intercepts, or did the intercepts you made of their radio transmissions, reveal whether they had any difficulties with their normal chains of command or not?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So generally would it appear -- did it appear to you that those with whom you were negotiating would have been able to contact those who were at the front line?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly they would.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And how far up the chain of command -- in your experience as a reserve officer, how far up the chain of command would communications about an attack of this kind have gone?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly the top leadership made the decisions, and they were just those who carried them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you say the top leadership, whereabouts would the top leadership be located?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: From the General Staff towards the units on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The General Staff being located in which town?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: In Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you have any doubts about whether communications that you intercepted or that you heard about with your negotiators would have reached Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: We listened in in the zone of responsibility within Dubrovnik municipality, so we didn't have access to communications beyond the Boka area and the Hercegovina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I understand that, but from your general knowledge of how communications worked and what you've told us, do you have any reason to doubt that in fact the communications went, as appropriate, to and from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: No. There was no reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to deal with the next paragraph as swiftly as I can. A few individuals: Svicevic, was one of the JNA negotiators, a psychiatrist by background. You've told us already of a ten-to-one threat. Was he the man who made that observation?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Svicevic, who in those days conducted the negotiations in the Supetar Hotel in Cavtat, at negotiations attended by representatives of the European Community, said the following: "In response to each of your shells, we will fire ten of ours." So in those days, the shells were flying over our heads, and the representative of the European Community counted them, but he couldn't bring any influence to bear over those developments.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And this ten-to-one threat, what type of shells were you firing and what type of shells were the JNA responding with?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: We first defended ourselves, and in our defence we did use 82-millimetre mortars, and they responded with howitzer guns of 155 and 130-millimetre calibre, exclusively shooting at civilian targets in the town of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was the same Colonel Svicevic the negotiator on the 19th of November where a cease-fire was being pressed for, including by the international representatives? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There had been fire coming from land-based positions in Konavle and from Trebinje as well as from the sea. And did Svicevic eventually concede to the cease-fire that was being pressed on him?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He agreed. He signed it. The author of the document was the then minister in the French government, Bernard Kouchner, but he signed it without having been authorised to do so, and he didn't appear again at the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As you understood it, the reason he was removed from the negotiations was what?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Due to the very fact that he didn't have the authority, the authorisation, to sign that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was he then replaced as lead negotiator by a retired Belgrade colonel, part of whose name is Radojevic?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How serious was he in attempting to achieve negotiation, as you judged it?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: He was appointed merely as a figurehead. An elderly gentleman who couldn't find his bearings in time or space, he had been called back from retirement. He had probably been reactivated. However, other men really conducted the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was one of those men called Sofronije Jeremic, a Frigate Captain?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Though a mere captain, your impression was that he was in fact acting in what capacity?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Frigate Captain Sofronije Jeremic was a top-level intelligence officer in the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally, on the topic of negotiations, after the next attack on Dubrovnik to which we'll turn, were you aware on the 5th of December of negotiations between Croatian ministers and Admiral Jokic about which you can answer questions, if asked?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before the next attack, on the 6th of December, had you intercepted JNA radio communication relating to a forthcoming attack?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: On the 3rd of December, at the command post in Kupari, a decision was taken on another attack on Dubrovnik, and we intercepted their radio communications in which they were informing their units that the army had received approval for attack, an attack on Dubrovnik. So before the Croatian negotiators arrived in Cavtat. And at that same time, Admiral Brovet had negotiated -- arranged the meeting. When I say "at the same time," I mean that same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Shall we turn next to the attack on the 6th of December. I've been using the world "old town" but I think you prefer to describe the old town as "the monument" or "protected monument"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were there to protect human lives, human lives in Lapad, Gruz, Ploce, and in the old town in Mokosica was of equal value.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. The attack on the 6th of December, can you remember what hour it started, how long it lasted?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: The attack started at 5.55 or 57 minutes, and it lasted until the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was this an attack on the old town or the protected monument, as you call it, or was it more widely focused?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: It was first focused on the Srdj fortress. However, at 0700 hours, a part of the attack turned towards the town of Dubrovnik itself, including the historical monument of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, to what extent were civilians subject of attack or subject to targeting?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: The very fact that about 30 civilians were killed on that day and not a single soldier speak for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The positions from which the attack came gave what sort of view of the old town with what sort of opportunity to see whether it was civilians who were suffering or not?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: They could indeed see. They set out from a couple of positions. First, they had artillery preparation that was coming from Konavle and Carina, which is on the border of Bosnia-Herzegovina, with howitzer guns of 150 centimetres, and then with 130 millimetre shells - this was artillery attacks - and then infantry attacks started towards the Srdj fortress. The forward command post, as it was called, was at the plateau of Zarkovica, and the person who coordinated the attack was a battleship captain Milan Zec who was at the forward command post, according to the terms they used.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you complain about this attack and what was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mike, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you complain about this attack? Did Jokic have something to say about it?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: We established contact for Minister Jurak with Admiral Jokic on two occasions, who first denied the events around Dubrovnik, saying that he knew nothing about them, and then in the third conversation with Mr. Rudolf, he said he would do everything for the attack to stop, but this was four hours into the attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
