utterances.text: Help us with this, would you, Mr. Simunovic: What was your position? We know that you were a member of the Territorial Defence. Can you tell us what your position was and what you were doing on the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a member of the command for the defence of Dubrovnik. In those days, we didn't just perform our own tasks but everything else as well. In fact, I was even one of the assistant commanders, that is, of General Marinovic. I had a colonel -- the rank of colonel in the Croatian army, head of the information service, and in those days, I also formed the military police in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It says -- the transcript obviously needs correcting. Four hours into the attack that Jokic said the attack would stop. Did it stop immediately after he said it would stop, or did it carry on after that?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: It didn't stop immediately but about an hour later. But there was sporadic shelling of Dubrovnik even after the official cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The following day, did the JNA admit or deny that damage was done?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: The next day, at negotiations which I did not attend, they did not deny those events in Dubrovnik. And at that joint meeting at which, in quotation marks, the agreement on a cease-fire was signed, they requested that permission be given, following orders from General Kadijevic, for two officers of the Yugoslav People's Army to visit Dubrovnik and a cameraman from Belgrade, for them to see for themselves the truth of the allegations, that is, whether Dubrovnik had been shelled or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I think we needn't take this in any detail. You were the officer who went and, in circumstances that may have been rather alarming, met the JNA officers on the Rijeka Dubrovacka, took them back, I think, to the old town where they, in plain clothes, videoed the damage that could be seen, and a cameraman working for your units took a video of the same objects they were seeing, so that we're in a position to play, in a couple of minutes, the video that was taken on your behalf, the video from time to time showing the JNA video operators filming the same things that you were also filming; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Regarding this video recording that we made, I can say that that is so. But the other one I haven't seen. It was made by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we come to that, there's Exhibit 370, tab 3, excerpt 15, I think queued up in the video booth. And if it is, it's a very short clip from the video seen yesterday. The Chamber, I hope, has the transcript before it. If we could just see that minute or so of video played, this witness can identify the person speaking. So Exhibit 370, tab 3, excerpt 15, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "This is part of the scenario that was prepared from the beginning and is now being implemented. Endeavouring to accuse the Yugoslav People's Army of failing to respect monuments of culture and the world cultural heritage such as the old town of Dubrovnik was, they prepared and are preparing in the town itself mine pits which they are activating, upon which they are issuing reports that the Yugoslav People's Army is shelling the old town."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two points: Do you recognise the person speaking? That's all we need from that. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Any truth in what he was saying?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, just give me a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see a longer excerpt yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It appears, Your Honour, we've actually got the wrong excerpt.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you shown a longer film yesterday of various people speaking about events in Dubrovnik, various JNA people? Was there one of those soldiers who you did identify or were able to identify?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who was it?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: General Damjanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what position did he hold? In what circumstances did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: He was a deputy commander of the Hercegovina Corps with the rank of colonel, and the commander of the Hercegovina Corps had the rank of general.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see anything of or have anything to do with Damjanovic in the course of negotiations or in the course of these attacks on Dubrovnik, or did you know him from before?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know General Damjanovic from before. We met in November in Mokosica in Dubrovnik. He headed the negotiating team in Mokosica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the video that you saw of him yesterday, if you can remember, what was it that he was saying? If not, we'll try and find it before the end of your testimony in order that you can deal with it. Can you remember what he was saying on the video?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's move, then, to the longer video. It's, I think, ten or 15 minutes, but it shows the damage to Dubrovnik, and it, I think, is probably worth expending that much time on it. May it be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's Prosecutor's Exhibit 372.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When the video booth is ready, can they start playing it. And I'd ask that the witness give some commentary as we're going along, but I'll try and trigger by the odd question the commentary he should make.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us as we're going along, please, Mr. Simunovic, what we're seeing.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: The church of St. Vlaho in the old part of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see damage there to the balustrade?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The entrance to the church of St. Vlaho. The damaged plaster and the fence destroyed. A shell that fell on Stradun.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is all in the old town or monument?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Here?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: A street. And this gentleman to the right was the cameraman from Belgrade who was sent upon instructions from General Kadijevic. A shell hit. This is one of the officers of the Yugoslav army. This is a second officer. We identified one of him. His name is Dragisa Perisic, a lawyer, a colonel by rank, coming from Kumbor, and this other one probably came from Belgrade. Again, this is Stradun and the shell that fell there. Roofs. There were few that remained intact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Red Cross on that building?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: This is the belfry of the Franciscan monastery. This is the cameraman from Belgrade. It was natural that no one in Dubrovnik knew who these gentlemen were. We had to provide for their security. That was the promise that we had given.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This was the day after the attack in which how many people had been killed?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. This is the second day of the attack, because there was an attack on the 6th. On the 7th, there were negotiations, and this was on the 8th. About 30 civilians were killed. You can see from the facades that phosphorous shells were used which caused fires, as you can see now. The building of the Dubrovnik festival that burnt. This is the Stradun again. A second burnt-down building next to the festival building. A water tap, fountain. The entrance to the Franciscan monastery. The cloister of this monastery.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where are we here?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: The stone fence of the Franciscan monastery, the plasterwork destroyed completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And now we're inside?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: The inside of the monastery. One officer, the second officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think we just saw a picture of you, but we missed it. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was the one in uniform between the two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Shell damage grooves, we can see?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: The stone balustrades. The oldest pharmacy in Europe. In the cloister of the Dominican -- I'm sorry, of the Franciscan monastery. Direct hits.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pause there just for a minute, if you could, please. Now, we've spoken of Srdj, a fortress above the town. What are we looking at here?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Just above the minaret tower, to the left you can see the Srdj fortress. Above the minaret tower, to the left. It's a bad shot but you can discern it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can see how high it is above Dubrovnik. I never got you to deal with this in detail, but in fact you never lost it to the JNA because although you thought they'd taken it, you came to realise at one stage that they had not in fact taken it, so an evacuation that your troops had made off Srdj was then followed by a retaking of it; would that be correct? Just say yes if I've got it roughly right and you can give detail, if asked, later.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: If we're talking about the 6th, we're now looking at the photos on the 8th, they did try to capture Srdj fortress, but they failed to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's press on with the video, please.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: This is inside the Franciscan monastery. This is a window through which the shell flew in, and I passed by six seconds before. There was another that fell through, and another that didn't explode. This is a 120-millimetre shell. This is what I personally collected; 190 pieces, smaller and larger ones. This is from November.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There you are in uniform?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am. The cameraman from Belgrade. This is Brother Jozo Softar, the Friar. This is the library.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By good fortune it didn't burn, I think you'll see.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Could this be translated?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "This is one of the most important libraries in the former Yugoslavia, in the whole of Europe, keeping documents of all the peoples and cultures. They're not important only for Dubrovnik and Croatia, but even for Serbia and Montenegro and Macedonia. These are documents that are being treasured here for ages. And you see what happened. For a moment, we thought it was on fire, because people saw smoke. There was terrible smoke coming out of here. However, fortunately, it didn't burn. Seventy thousand books are kept here."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Jozo Softar recognised these two officers. He was the only one who recognised them. The other people that you see are the security for these officers. The Jadran restaurant, or St. Klara.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you remember where we are here?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: We see a house that has been burnt. You will recognise the effects of phosphorous. The yellow traces are the result of phosphorous. The Siroka Street or Broad Street. A house burnt down in that street. The next house that was burnt. For the sake of explanation, 2.000 shells fell on the protected monument of the old town in the period from the 1st of October up to this day and inclusive of this day. This is a house burnt across the street from the Orthodox church in Dubrovnik. We're now on the ramparts that encircle the town of Dubrovnik, and from them you have the best view of Dubrovnik's roofs, few of which were left intact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The ramparts themselves, I think, were damaged, as we'll see in the next minutes.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were. This is the Imperial hotel that was burnt in the month of November. This is the -- on the 11th of December, there was an attack and this hotel was burnt down. This is the university centre that we still see smoke coming out of, and that was hit and was set on fire. A shell that hit this area. The shells themselves. This is the European Commission. The European Community and the roofs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's another view of Srdj, is it?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. This is Srdj fortress.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is part of the ramparts?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's right. Just by way of explanation, Dubrovnik was targeted from three directions with the 130-millimetre guns from the Dubrovnik airport area, from Zarkovica and Bosanki Sticeva [phoen]. And from Careva with the 155-millimetre howitzer-type weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The airport is on the road down to Montenegro. Zarkovica is the east?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Zarkovica is east. And from Zarkovica you have a view over the entire town centre, and that was where the forward command post was located. This is the parking lot underneath the ramparts, the walls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just pause -- perhaps pause the video there for a second and go back to look at those cars again, if we could. And what happened in the area where those cars were parked? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: The owners of these cars thought that they would be best protected in the car parks right by the town wall. But as you can see from this image, that's precisely where the shells fell, and all the cars were burnt. There and in other places too, and you'll be able to see that on the footage as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Continue on, please. Continue the video.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: I must emphasise that we're looking at the protective monument of Dubrovnik, the old town. However, the whole of the town of Dubrovnik was shelled equally intensively. The Lapad area, the Gruz area, Ploce; they suffered the same fate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think we're coming towards the end, but we should just play it for completeness since it's a single exhibit.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: This is the Dominican monastery. Zarkovica's up there. You can see Zarkovica on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... view it afforded of the town, yes?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: These are the boats that were destroyed in the old harbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Which is on the east of the old town, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. This is a bit of tape that had been used before, and we come back to the...

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: These are the vessels that were destroyed at the Podporella [phoen], as we call it, in the old town. A phosphorous shell. The ramparts and walls. The old town harbour. The cars in the harbour and the remains of a shell. A shell that hit the belfry. Ships burnt to a singe. We used this boat to take us to the negotiations in Cavtat actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Even when on the boat, were you occasionally shelled, fired at?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: On three occasions. They fired at us three times and in fact hit us once. We were not alone. With us were representatives of the international community and the United Nations representatives as well. This is the Dubrovnik cathedral.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Another short extract from the film that is being played over, and then we come towards the end. Just carry on, please. Very well. That's the end. Thank you very much. A few concluding questions, please, Mr. Simunovic. From the first to last, had the forces defending Croatia initiated any offensive action against the JNA?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, they had not. Since -- they did not launch any offensive action against the JNA. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who had been the first victims of the conflict that was played out in the Dubrovnik area; Croats or Serbs or who?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: The Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By this time, by the attack on the 6th of December, what was the roughly maximum number of men defending Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: The number was about 300 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were any of those deployed in the old town, in the monument, as you call it, on any of the occasions when that part of Dubrovnik was attacked?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: The military positions were outside the old town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You told us about the weaponry you had obtained from the island of Korcula with the missing bits. Did you manage to get that weaponry into working order by December?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: We did manage, but what we produced, unfortunately, wasn't of any long duration. It was just for one-time use.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Had you managed to obtain any other heavy weaponry between the time when you got that equipment from Korcula in December and the end of this part of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: When we look at December, and by December we had not managed to get any heavy weaponry into Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. After allowing the JNA to film in the way that we've now seen, was Dubrovnik attacked again or not?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what period?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout the whole of -- if we're talking up to 1992, then there were sporadic attacks throughout the conflict until the Yugoslav army left Croatia, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you wait there, you'll be asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, the tape that you just played prompts me to raise a particular question. Dubrovnik is a city that is, of course, well known for its beauty and general historical interest. Is there any evidence as to whether certain sites in Dubrovnik had been recognised by UNESCO as sites that were to be preserved for historical purposes? I don't know whether you have any evidence as to that, but I think it would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think this witness could probably help us with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Simunovic?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: The old town, all of the old town, makes up the cultural heritage and monuments and are protected as such. It has been recorded as such, I think, where records of that kind are kept, that is to say, the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Summarised in paragraph 6. If the Chamber wants further documentation in support of the proposition that it's a completely protected site, we may be able to find it, but that's certainly my understanding. The witness confirms it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It might be as well if you produce the documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Fine, very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simunovic, you began your testimony by describing the conflicts and clashes that took place in the Prevlaka region. Could you tell us when that was exactly?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: The conflict began as of the 26th of September and went up to the 1st of October, but if you mean the clashes and if you mean to say that we targeted Yugoslav army positions, then my answer is that we did not because we neither had the power and force or manpower.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what I'm thinking of, and I assume you know as you're an officer yourself that at the Prevlaka area, there was the JNA base there. That's where it was located, and the JNA installations as well, radar installations and other facilities.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the conflict actually began in the following way: Your forces attacked the JNA installations there, did they not?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, they did not. Mr. Milosevic, I assume you were not there then, in the area then, and had you been there, you wouldn't have made that assumption and brought it up now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's just clarify that point, because according to the information that I have, that's how it was. That's what my information tells me. You said that Dubrovnik was attacked by a corps, and then you went on to enumerate several battalions, and then you mentioned tank units, the navy, the air force. Now, explain this to me: As a professional yourself, as an officer yourself, how is it possible that if the JNA had such vast potential and strength as you said and wanted to take control of Dubrovnik, how come it didn't?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't any special army. They just had the strength to do so and power but they didn't have the courage and bravery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you were successful in defending it from all that. Now, did it ever occur to you that they never actually wanted to take control of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: That didn't occur to us, either to myself or my colleagues, because had they not wanted to, they wouldn't have looted, burnt houses and killed civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And do you know that there was an order of the 4th of October of the General Staff - I quoted its numbers here - in which it is strictly stated that Dubrovnik should not be taken control of nor should it be shelled from the ground, from the air, or from the sea.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure you ought to know the outcome of the other side. I don't know about that order, but I do know what happened; I experienced it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And for you, the very fact perhaps that General Kadijevic, at that time the Defence Minister and the number one man leading the army, sent an inspection team to Belgrade to take footage of the consequences of those operations and actions. Is that a -- is it logical for you to assume that the reports that he was given stated that Dubrovnik should not be shelled and the order should be respected for the non-attack of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, it's not logical, and I'll explain why. Because General Kadijevic, as the Supreme Commander of that particular army, should have known what was going on, what had been going on the previous two months in Dubrovnik. So that wasn't the first time that Dubrovnik was shelled. Dubrovnik was shelled equally intensively in October and November, but as we have just -- as we're mentioning General Kadijevic, I must also say that he was informed. He knew very well of a meeting that took place in Kupari at the command post on the 3rd of December and that a decision was made once again to attack Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's what you claim. I have no information about that. Now, before I move on to another area, tell me, what does Serbia have to do at all with that conflict of yours around Dubrovnik, your conflict with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I should probably be asking you that question because are better versed in matters of that kind than I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, precisely because I am better versed, I can tell you that Serbia has nothing to do with the events around Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: According to what I know on my information and my facts and figures that we analysed when we looked at the situation, we did link you up with everything that was going on in and around Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How were you able to link anybody from Serbia with what was going on in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about Serbs and Serbia, I'm talking about you personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how are you able to link me up to anything that was going on in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you will recall, I'm sure, that you holidayed in Kupari, you took your summer holidays there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, of course I did, and for ten years in Kupari in the President Hotel and in some other hotels in the Dubrovnik area and I liked spending my holidays there very much. And had it been up to me, not a single stone would have fallen from Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm happy to hear that, but something else went on again, when we looked at the security situation, and we were a young army, we were a fledgling army being formed, but from -- we did know a little about life generally and what was going on and we tried to see who the people were because they were war times, times of war, and we had to see who it was who came in the two or three years prior to the outbreak of the conflict to do business around Dubrovnik. Let me link this up, link you up and the Yugoslav army up. Not Serbia and the Serbs but you and the Yugoslav army, let's link it up to the whole situation. And I'm sure you will recall that in 1989 -- let's take the year 1989, for example. I have no personal knowledge of this, I wasn't there, but that was the information I received, and it's interesting information, that you yourself in one of your sojourns and visits to the old town or the restaurant, a restaurant called the Sarajevo restaurant, Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're talking about a restaurant?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You went to that restaurant with your friends. And on that occasion in 1989, your security detail were military personnel from Kupari. The SUP or Ministry of the Interior or the police force at the time, you didn't allow them to provide your safety and security as was customary when people came to Dubrovnik, but you -- your security detail was from the army. They were army personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, come on, Mr. Simunovic. Nobody provided security for me in Dubrovnik whenever I visited. I would go with my young son, with my daughter, with my wife, and my friends, friends, local Dubrovnik people, and I would visit the patisserie in the Siroka Street and stroll around the Stradun, the main street, and I had no security details from Serbia or anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm talking about 1989, and that's how it was in 1989. You did have your security force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, you have the wrong information, but I don't want to waste time on that. What I want to ask you is this, and I have a large number of questions to ask you, in fact. You say on page 2, paragraph 2 of your statement that at the end of 1990 and 1991, that violence came to a head and that it became clear that the JNA would help the rebellion of the Serbs in Croatia. That's what you write in your statement. Why did the Serbs rebel at all in Croatia in that year of 1990?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: I can only speak about the Dubrovnik region.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you're making a general statement, a sweeping statement.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: When I said that, I meant Dubrovnik and the Dubrovnik area itself. And as you know, at the first democratic elections that were held -- or I don't know if you know about this at all but I assume you do because you knew quite a lot of things, in Dubrovnik two Serbian parties were formed, the so-called Yugoslav Democratic Party and the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me explain it to you because this is an answer to your question, part of my answer to your question. Those gentlemen, with every right, organised themselves, went out to the elections, and they fared as they fared. However, afterwards when the results were what they were, they began to deal in -- to think about intensively of contacts, and they attempted in Dubrovnik on two occasions -- they went to Podgorica, actually, to see Mr. Kostic who was I think the vice premier of that state at the time, or vice-president, and they wanted to intervene. They said they were in jeopardy and that they wanted to dislocate from Dubrovnik. So these were sort of indicators at that time in the town of Dubrovnik what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you have any information as to them going to Belgrade and seeking contacts in Belgrade with anybody?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: They went to Trebinje and they went to Podgorica, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they went to the neighbouring areas, the neighbouring republics, Bosnia-Herzegovina and Montenegro, I assume.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I suppose to people who thought the same way as they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, quite probably. They felt they could get assistance because they felt themselves to be in jeopardy. Now, in view of the general situation, tell me this, please: You say that in Croatia the Serbs rebelled. Tell me why they rebelled. We mentioned the numerous constitutional changes that took place, the dismissals from work, liquidations and so on, all this that went on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the witness has already answered that he's dealing with the people in Dubrovnik. If you want to ask him about that, you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this general atmosphere that prevailed, and on the 13th of March, 1990, it was the former government of that former Socialist Republic of Croatia that sent a letter to the federal government and the governments of the other republics in which it condemned the events, both those at the general Sabor Assembly of the HDZ party as well as the Petrova Gora meeting, and they appealed to the population for cooperation and joint undertakings to prevent the further disintegration of good neighbourly relations. That was the government of the day in Croatia. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't link it up to Dubrovnik, and that's why I'm here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And do you know that at these free elections that you mention in 1990, for the most part the Serbs in Croatia voted for Racan's party, the party of Racan, the League of Communists, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The last couple of minutes of time have been occupied with questions that the Court has indicated and that the witness has now indicated are outside the scope of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And it's just wasting time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Move on to something he can deal with.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I can move on quite quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, in view of all the events, tell me who provoked the violence. Because you know full well that at the time these newly established paramilitary formations in Croatia took over the JNA barracks and killed the soldiers and officers in them. Is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Milosevic, we're going to come to Dubrovnik or we're simply not going to get on with this. Now, if you've got questions about Dubrovnik, you can ask them. You can ask other witnesses about other parts of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us concentrate on Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simunovic, you say on page 2, paragraph 3 of your statement that the Serbs were over-represented in the key organs and institutions of the municipalities, including Dubrovnik. That's what you say. And this seems to be a free assessment on your part, because you enumerate the posts, for example, the notary, the president of the courts, the head of the customs office. What other important posts were held by Serbs in Dubrovnik and did they, holding those functions, jeopardise the positions of anybody or, rather, the position of the Croats in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: No. I just tried to explain to the investigators the situation as it stood in Dubrovnik and which we found ourselves in in 1990 and 1991, regardless of the fact that these gentlemen happened to be of a different religion, because they were Croats of a different religion. I would say they were Croats but of a different religion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They held all the key posts in Dubrovnik and you know that full well yourself because you had a lot of friends there, you walked around there.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Not among any high-ranking officials, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The statement is available if the Court wants it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think we need it at the moment. If we need it, we'll ask for it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 2, paragraph 3, you say that you do not recall that a single Serb was attacked or bothered in any way. However, that's not true. Look at the tasks of the police station of Cavtat in the first half of 1991, for example, where, among other things, the task was realised to topple -- to destroy Serb houses or, as it says, the houses that were unlawfully built, especially Serb houses. This is a police report from Cavtat where a citizen informs the police station that as a sniper he would shoot so that they would know who was shooting. Or, for example, a 15th of August report of 1991 in which one woman is complaining that the guards are disturbing her throughout the night and that there was shooting during the night every night. Do you know anything about information of this kind, reports of this kind?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, I do not, and they're not truthful.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, because you say they're not truthful, I am going to give you this or show you this, the tasks performed in the course of 1991, the destruction of unlawfully built houses, especially Serb houses - I underlined this - and the monitoring and quest for individuals, particularly those linked to the JNA, taking away the Adriatic vessel and children's holiday homes owned by Belgrade, and action against the JNA. So this is an original document that I have here. It is from Cavtat, and it is dated 1991. One of your own documents. I would like to tender it into evidence and show you the document.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: If Their Honours permit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can we just do one thing at a time. Where does the document come from, Mr. Milosevic? Is it said to be a police document or what is it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a police document, yes. I was quoting from it. And this is the photocopy of the original, and it comes from Croatia, Mr. May. It was not fabricated in Serbia. You can check it out on the document itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us -- let the witness see the document. Then he can comment on it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For example, the second point, it is the report by the duty officer of the police station of Cavtat on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will deal with one thing at a time. Now, the witness has the document, this police report, and he can comment on it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document as a document is -- has no value or worth. It hasn't got a title. It hasn't got an ending. So regardless of the sources that Mr. Milosevic might have, I have my doubts as to the authenticity of this document. But if -- with the Court's indulgence, I can comment on part of what it says in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What it says here and is linked to the destruction of Serb houses, I can say the following: After the advent of democratic power in Dubrovnik, both Croatian and Serbian houses were destroyed which had not been constructed on the basis of the necessary construction permits. They were illegally -- had been illegally erected in the first place. But decisions for their destruction were written out, and this was done on the basis of a document. Nobody did it because they felt like it. Now, what I can see from this particular piece of paper, one would not be able to conclude that it was an authentic document at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you're denying it, but we'll prove that it is authentic. I mentioned another report, and it is a telex, a police telex --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll come to that one. We'll deal with this one first. Let the Court just have a look at it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to draw your attention to the fact that there is the word "particularly". Pulling down houses but especially Serbian houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what you're saying is being proven false by this expression that we find in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us deal with this first. Just a moment, Mr. Milosevic. Stop interrupting while we deal with this. Yes. What we'll do with this first document, since there is a dispute about its authenticity, is we'll mark it for identification. The Prosecution can have a look, and if they have objections, they can raise it in due course. We'll get a number for it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Defence Exhibit 79 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Here is a report of the officer on duty in the Cavtat police station on the 16th of August, 1991, in the period from 0600 to 1400 hours. That is his shift. And among other things, it says: "Mijo Kurajica came to report that today around 1600 hours at Brdo in Brotnice, he would fire his sniper rifle so that it would be known who was firing. He said he would also inform our reservists at Brdo. There were no other developments. Signed Ivica Handzek." So the officer on duty in Cavtat. I will give you that document too because I've grouped several questions together. On the 15th of August, 1991, there was an orgy with Russian ladies, shooting by reserve guardsmen from Cilipi who spend every night there. So I asked you about the shooting of a sniper and the wild parties by guardsmen at Cilipi. And you also have the reports of your policemen on duty from Cavtat signed - this one is signed by Niksa Bender, the previous one by Ivica Handzek - and they can also be verified whether they were the people who were the officers on duty at that time. Obviously by their names and surnames, they are Croats, so please look at these two Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. documents too and then we can move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I proceed, Mr. May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness see the document, just see the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Please look at them.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: First in connection with the document signed by Mr. Ivica Handzek. If this is authentic, Mr. Kurajica Mijo acted in accordance with the law. You probably know that in Konavle there are many huntsmen, and I think that the fact that he came to the police station to report the use of a sniper cannot be used for any kind of construed allegations. As for the second report signed by Mr. Niksa Bender, you didn't mention the sequence but that there was shooting by reservists in Cilipi who spend every night there. The two cannot be linked together, you see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No. I'm giving you different examples.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, of course it's up to you to do that and it's up to me to comment. So I've commented on this first document signed by Mr. Kurajica. As for the authenticity of this document, especially the parts highlighted by you, I could not agree at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But the document is authentic, sir.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I, know and probably you too, every document needs to have some kind of a header. Anyone could have written this and signed it. Regardless of what we were like, we were, after all, an organised community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will do the same with those three documents. They will be exhibited together and given the next -- just a moment. They will be given the next exhibit number and marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the report of the officer signed by Mr. Handzek, dated 16 August 1991 will be Defence Exhibit 80 marked for identification. And then the report, or the letter signed by Mr. Bender dated 15th August, 1991 will be Defence Exhibit 81 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'm afraid our time will be limited, so I have to hurry up. Do you know the names of Judges Dragan Gajic and Bruno Karnincic from Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that they carried out most of the on-site inspections in the Dubrovnik region regarding the destruction of the property of the local Serbs?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that according to the reports they made on the spot, more than 50 houses, mostly located in Zupa, Cavtat, and the surroundings, and in other places of the same region, which belonged to local Serbs, inhabitants, citizens of Croatia, were destroyed in various bomb attacks when various explosive devices were used. There are statements -- the official statement of the Judge given to the investigator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness doesn't know anything about the reports but he can be asked whether he knows anything about the bombing or the use of explosives against the houses of local Serbs. Now, Mr. Simunovic, do you know anything about that allegation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know anything, but I do know Mr. Gajic, and I know Mr. Karnincic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you assume that their reports, submitted officially, were authentic?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Of course I didn't work in the judiciary, so I didn't have insight into those things, but knowing the first gentleman, I don't think that would be possible under any circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And had you ever heard of explosives being thrown into the houses of local Serbs through the window, mostly when their occupants were not there, and that in three cases during such attacks, the tenants were seriously wounded? This is also contained in a report of the Judge.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, which Judge?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Dragan Gajic. Do you know Mr. Gajic?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But I'm showing you documents that I received from the opposite side, not from any Belgrade office but from the opposing side which examined you a moment ago. Do you know that Mr. Gajic needed to report -- make such a report where he was working? And I assume he did, as there are 50 such reports, according to this information.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Believe me, in those days we took special care not to hurt any single loyal citizen of Croatia of a different faith. Similarly, we believe that we succeeded in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, only in Serbia was care taken not to offend citizens of any nationality throughout those ten years. I don't know that that was the case elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going to adjourn now. We've come to a suitable moment. Mr. Milosevic, in relation to your last questions, the witness statement for Mr. Gajic, of course, has already been exhibited. So it would seem pointless to go over what he has said with this witness who doesn't know anything about it. You may want to use your time more usefully. We will adjourn now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we've considered the time available, and in this case you have up to one and a half hours left if you need it, or if you want it, of cross-examination with this witness, which means we won't finish him today. We will have to ask him to come back tomorrow. We will go on until quarter to two on the examination, and then we'll come back to deal with the point about the documents which have been served on you, the matter you raised earlier. Now, if you'd like to go on with your examination.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- by instructions of the local authorities and the president of the local court, Marinko Peric, they were released from prison and the joint paramilitary formations in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises. We did not hear the beginning of the sentence. Witness, microphone, please. Microphone for the witness, please. We apologise, we didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you repeat that, Mr. Simunovic. It wasn't translated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As one of the organisers of the defence of Dubrovnik, I am not aware of those data.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since we have -- I have here a list of civilians killed from the area of Dubrovnik, do you know and is my information correct that there were about 150 post-mortems of persons who were mostly wearing Croatian military uniforms, and the pathologist was Dr. Ciganovic?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: That is not true. The exact number of killed Croatian soldiers is 103.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You say that Risto Vrica, a senior official of the DB in Dubrovnik, organised the Serb nationalist activities in town. What kind of activities did he organise?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: That is not what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't mention him.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: I did mention him, but what you just said I didn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what the question was, and I don't know the context, but probably it's a problem of translation or the interpretation of the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then it probably is a problem due to translation and interpretation of the text. You say that in the summer of 1991, the HDZ in Dubrovnik formed a Crisis Staff. Why was a Crisis Staff formed in Dubrovnik in the summer of 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: An error again. The Crisis Staff of Dubrovnik municipality was formed by the elected authorities, which means that it was not a party Crisis Staff. Now, why it was formed, you probably are aware of the events within the territory of the former Yugoslavia in the summer of 1991; it was formed to take care of the civilian population of Dubrovnik municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And detachment of the National Guards Corps was formed at the same time, and since you're saying that no one ever thought it would be possible for a conflict to break out, why were they being armed and why were they formed, this detachment?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: As you know, the National Guard Corps was a part of the Ministry of the Interior, and the Ministry of the Interior formed the National Guards Corps. Now, why? For the defence, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I have here quite a number of exhibits, and if it will take too much time, I don't know whether I can give each of them to you individually or all of them together, but for instance, look at, please, Dubrovnik, the 15th of February, 1991. February 1991. To the president of the Municipal Assembly, the president for -- of the commission for appointments of the Municipal Assembly. Reference is made to the appointment of the Chief of Staff for the Territorial Defence, and it says: "This year, the Territorial Defence is gradually becoming operational." This was dated in February 1991. Nothing was happening. There were no attacks. Isn't this an obvious example of the militarisation of Dubrovnik in those days, as early as February 1991? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, it is not right. The Territorial Defence started to be organised in August 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But please look at this document. I hope it is an original document. Zeljko Pavlovic, the TO commander, signed it. It has a number on top, 44/1, 15th of February, 1991. Is this an authentic document? Please tell me.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Probably it is authentic, but it doesn't say that the Territorial Defence was formed as of this date. I told you in August 1991. This is a request, probably a request. I don't have time nor does the Court have time to read through this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But I am asking you isn't this evidence of the militarisation of Dubrovnik as early as February 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, that is not evidence that Dubrovnik was being militarised in February 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Simunovic, perhaps since the matter is being raised, you better just read that to yourself, if you would, and tell us what it's about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now that I have read it, I am able to see that this was a normal procedure undertaken in peacetime, because there was a Chief of Staff, and the Chief of Staff probably took up some other duty, and now there's a normal procedure to appoint a new one. He existed before, and the request was made for a new one because the previous one had left his post. And I think this is fully in compliance with the legal procedure of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that at the very beginning of 1991, you were calling up the reserve force?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: That is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But I have here an original form of a statement of one of the reservists, and as an attachment you have the document on an issuance of his rifle, automatic rifle and pistol, and it is dated the 14th of January, 1991. Is this an authentic document? Please look at it and tell me. So the 14th of January, 1991. The form of the statement and then a receipt for the weapons and ammunition and equipment that he had received, and everything else. Is this an original document?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: This document does not relate to the Territorial Defence. This document refers to the Ministry of Internal Affairs, which means that it was within its jurisdiction. And most probably, though I cannot claim it, it may have been a member of the National Guards Corps which at that time was under the Ministry of Internal Affairs. So the Territorial Defence and this document that you are tendering are not compatible. The two don't go together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the National Guard Corps was not an armed force that was being formed in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: The National Guards Corps was a part of the Ministry of the Interior, that is, a part of the police and not of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what is the difference if we're talking about armed formations?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: The difference is considerable. Armed formations and the Territorial Defence is the military component and the National Guards Corps is a civilian or police component.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But it cannot really be said that everything started with the alleged conflict with the army, because all these things were happening in January 1991, because the same people acquired more important weapons later on. Look at the receipt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If that document could be handed in. Is there a second document there?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: For instance, Antun Kovacevic, issued with an automatic rifle, number so-and-so, and a bag with four clips of ammunition, and the fifth is fitted onto the rifle. And 190 bullets. This is dated the 7th of May, 1991. Would you like to look at that?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: If it is an identical document, there's no need, simply no need, because this is not linked to the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But is it linked to the fact that weapons and ammunition was being distributed from the beginning of 1991 in the territory of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Accused, I would like to ask you here before Their Honours not to produce evidence that is not evidence at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, now, Mr. Simunovic, it's a matter for us to say what's evidence. We'll have these documents exhibited now, the three that have been put in. Before we do, is there anything you want to say about that final one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I would. I do apologise, Your Honour. There's a photocopy of the official ID of a member of the reserve police force. So this refutes everything that the accused has said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is just due to circumstances that it happens to be on the same piece of paper. But the name on the receipt for the rifle is Antun and not this other one that is mentioned on the same piece of paper. Very well. Tell me please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's deal with these documents first. It's been suggested that it's a receipt for a rifle on that document, Mr. Simunovic. Can you help us as to what these documents are? Do you want to say anything more about them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall try. Simply, in those days, I was not a member of the Territorial Defence or of the armed forces. But reading through this document and these dates, it is visible that all these members who were issued rifles were members of the reserve police of the Ministry of the Interior and that there is nothing strange that they should be issued short- and long-barreled weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Were they issued such weapons in times of peace, as a matter of course?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in peacetime, they were issued an automatic rifle and 200 bullets of ammunition?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Probably units of the National Guards Corps had this envisaged by their regulations and rules.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you please admit this into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going to do that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simunovic, is it true --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a moment while we deal with this. I think we'll admit them. If there is any objection in the future, we'll deal with it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the letter or the document for Zeljko Pavlovic dated 15 February, 1991 will be marked Defence Exhibit 82. The statement of the reservist dated 14 of January, 1991 and the receipt Defence Exhibit 83. And the receipt issuing the rifle to Antun Kovacevic dated 7 May, 1991, is Defence Exhibit 84.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Simunovic, is it true that you carried out wartime deployment on the 14th of January, 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: It is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that on the 24th of January, at the Dubrovnik airport, weapons were procured?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: That is not true either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Apart from obtaining large quantities of weapons via the airport, would you be kind enough to look at this request of Dubrovnik airport dated the 24th of January, and the official report of the police station. Work organisation Dubrovnik airport. This is an original document addressed to the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia, the secretariat of Dubrovnik municipality, request for weapons. "Allow us to obtain bullets for physical, technical protection through the Ribo Materijal company in Zagreb." And then there's a list of 25 men with automatic and semi-automatic rifles, and telephone numbers of the same, and then an Official Note from the frontier crossing at Dubrovnik, signed by Kemo Trsunovic, inspector, saying that on the 27th of June, 1991, Lujo Lasic came and asked for our assistance regarding the delivery of weapons at the Pleso airport in Zagreb. He was expecting a delivery of 40 pistols through Ribo Materijal. There is no other accompanying documents. All this is written in this report of the frontier crossing. This is the frontier service for affairs on the border at land and at sea. Will you please look at these documents and tell us whether they are authentic.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Regarding the first document, I can say, though I wasn't there at the time, that it is nothing unusual. As you know well, all airports in the world, including our own at Dubrovnik, had and will have a security service, and probably that is the source. Whether this was regular reinforcements of ammunition or not, one should ask the person who signed the document. I don't see anything strange. The security of all airports, including Dubrovnik airport, needed to exist. As for the official report, I see it for the first time, and I'm simply unable to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And could you then please comment on the report on state and problems of defence and proposals for strengthening it, signed by -- these are all documents from Croatia, signed by Marin Vukorep? Does the name ring a bell, Marin Vukorep?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know the name. But I also know, you have already repeated several times, this is intended exclusively for defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But see what he says under point 5: "Purchase and distribution of weapons and lethal means can be done by whoever wants to, without any records being kept or any information so that many criminal acts have already taken place." This is written in his report. And under paragraph 3: "No instructions for work, order and discipline exist so people are doing what they will." So look at this document too, please. It is also authentic. I hope you will not deny it. It is dated the 30th of August, 1991.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: A document without a header and without a signature, and who it is addressed to I cannot see, so simply, I am not able to comment on it. I cannot say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see, there is a signature.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. An information on the situation. To whom is this information addressed? And I don't see Mr. Vukarep's signature. So this could have been written at any time. I'm sorry, I can't comment. Please put it under a question mark. Take it and put it under a question mark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Assist us, Mr. Simunovic, so that we can follow. What is it supposed to be? What does it say it is, that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't read it. It consists of three pages, but I feel it necessary for me to say that if this is an official document, Mr. Vukorep was the chief of the Territorial Defence Staff, he was an official person, and such an official document he could only have sent to a superior body. However, from this document, without entering into the substance, I see that the document doesn't have a header nor a conclusion. So from this document, we cannot see who the document was addressed to and whether it was sent anywhere, without entering into the substance of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. That document can be marked for identification. The others should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the request of the Dubrovnik airport dated 24 January 1991, and the official report of the police station is Defence Exhibit 85. And the document signed by Mr. Vukorep dated 30 August 1991 is Defence Exhibit 86 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And now tell me this please, do you happen to know when the information was given that the national protection units had been Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. set up on the 1st of August, 30th of July, that the military facilities were switched off the urban network for electricity, water, et cetera? Are you aware of these orders? All this was happening on the 30th of July and up to the 8th of August. Take a look at this.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is the Republic of Croatia, the Ministry of Defence, the 30th of July, in the Ministry of Defence a National Protection Board was set up pursuant to an order by the Defence Minister. The telephones are mentioned, that the commander Antun Avramovic is designated, and then you have on the 30th of July the same thing, the Republic of Croatia, Defence Ministry, Zagreb, Opaticka 1 is the address, on the 30th of July; instructions for the work of the public protection organs for Croatia, establishing obstacles to military combat equipment, the setting up of teams to switch off the facilities of the Yugoslav People's Army from the utilities network, that is to say electricity, water, the PTT network, and to cut off all supplies to them and to organise the following companies, platoons, battalions numbering 30 -- 300 persons, brigades 3.000, et cetera, followed by an order for the staffs of the national protection organisation, and the date is the 30th of July for all of them. They have their numbers and everything else that they need to have.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but does all that refer to Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of course it does, yes.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: As you probably know, in the Dubrovnik area, in the Dubrovnik municipality, there were three positions held by the Yugoslav People's Army at that time. The Prevlaka, was anything cut off, the utilities? The island of Mljet, was anything cut off there? And on Sipan temporarily. So none the utility networks were cut off. This is probably a document of the Ministry of Defence. There's no reason that I should doubt that this is an authentic document, but I don't see anything negative, any negative points in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, does the document show that before any conflict took place you are militarising, arming, and positioning barricades, mines, explosives devices, et cetera, in this area and engaging in other activities related to combat operations?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean for attack or defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who were you preparing to defend yourselves against when nobody attacked you? Did anybody attack you on the 1st of January, 1991 or the 30th of June, 1991 perhaps?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Not us in Dubrovnik, no, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you happen to know of the following document, the Crisis Staff of the Dubrovnik municipality -- that is the title and header --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you want these documents exhibited?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Hand them in, please. We'll exhibit them. Exhibit them together.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That document will be Defence Exhibit 87, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Once again, a document. It says the Republic of Croatia, Dubrovnik municipality, Crisis Staff, the 6th of September of 1991, which was the time when you yourself say that nobody was attacking you. Mr. Zeljko Pavlovic, the commander of the TO headquarters of Dubrovnik. The subject is placing at the disposal of men and resources to the National Guards Corps of Dubrovnik. Then it goes on to say, sir, the Crisis Staff of the Dubrovnik municipality, at a meeting held on the 6th of December, decided - of course in 1991 - that manpower and technical and military materiel be placed at the disposal of the ZNG brigades, 116th Brigade, in the extent to which the commander sees necessary, finds necessary. Yes I've been asked to slow down. I shall do so. So the ZNG 116th Brigade, as required. And this is sent to the commander of the 116th ZNG Brigade. Milenko Bratus is the signatory with his signature. Take a look at this document and tell me if it is an authentic one, please. And to save the usher from going up and down twice, you set up a mines and explosive devices network on the same day. This is what it looked like in Vitaljina. And they are your own sketches and diagrams, in fact, with -- showing the network. It has been sketched in hand, showing a road where what has been planted and set up. So there's that too. Is that an authentic document?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: The first document is authentic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, just like the previous ones. And what about the second one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before we go on to these, just dealing with the first document from the Crisis Staff, placing, it said, men and resources at the disposal of the ZNG, is there any comment you wish to make about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I most certainly do. In order to be able to understand the purpose of all this, I have to spend a little time explaining it. A brigade. The 116th in this case. That is the 156th, actually, of the ZNG, that is to say the armed force of the Republic of Croatia, that is to say the Croatian army. I know, Your Honour, that this is a little complex because it came from the headquarters of the Territorial Defence. In this paper, we see what is being placed at the disposal are all these things as needed in the extent to which they are necessary. Believe me when I say we had -- we lacked everything, especially large territorial weapons which were in another republic belonging to the TO. What we were able to place at their disposal are long-barreled rifles, the ones that we had in the different work organisations, because the law applied of the former Yugoslavia where these work organisations needed to have protection platoons and certain weapons to man them, just like the people at the airport did. So this document is not disputed, and I see nothing in it that would be terrible in any way or negative in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Except for the fact that all this was going on at the end of June 1991, which is the time when you say you were not threatened by anyone.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Accused, do you really think that we didn't have the right to defend ourselves?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you're militarising the Dubrovnik area for which you claim had been demilitarised. So who is militarising it; you or the JNA?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: I do beg your pardon, but what are we militarising it with?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you spoke of guns, mortars, anti-aircraft guns and all the rest of it, all the other weapons yourself and the manpower and everything else, and here we have the issuance papers to the young men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can't mislead the witness in that way or try to mislead the Tribunal. He didn't speak of anti-aircraft guns. When you say that the document isn't disputed, what was the purpose of placing men and resources at the disposal of the ZNG? The accused says it was to militarise the area. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it is not militarisation. If it is militarisation, 30 to 50 men, if you call that militarisation per 125.000 or the number of inhabitants the Dubrovnik municipality had, or 6.000 or 7.000, can you speak of it as being militarisation at all? At the time, it was sort of a platoon, a protection company that the Ministry of the Interior tried to establish in Dubrovnik. After that, this grew to become a brigade of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Simunovic. But on that same day, take a look at the sketch there that I gave you. You drew a network for mines and explosive devices in Vitaljina and all the rest of it. They're your own documents. Is that how it was or not?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: I see this document for the first time here and now but I wish to comment on the document and say the following: As we made our assessments and evaluations, if not I myself personally then somebody else, but this is a document dating 2 September, we did know the forces that were amassing along the borders towards Croatia, and quite normally, we found it necessary to protect both Croatia and the Croatian population in the area. And not only did we mine this area, we also placed mines on all access roads, on all the approaches, and we did so, we placed the mines to prevent the army to advance into our own territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At that time, the army, as far as I remember, was deployed throughout the territory of Yugoslavia, and it was the Yugoslav People's Army all over the country. So it wasn't any advance any more, coming in from anywhere, it was on its own territory, the territory of Yugoslavia, and that was the middle of 1991. And the SFRY, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, was in existence at that time. Is that not so?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I really don't want to enter into polemics with you about that because it is not the topic of my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Fine. I'm just drawing your attention to those dates. Now, tell me this, please: Is it correct that your forces from the Vitaljina region, which you have there in front of you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I must just interrupt you for one moment. Have we finished with this document or do you want to ask some more questions about it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'd like to tender both those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let's just deal with the second one. Mr. Simunovic, it's alleged that you drew that document. Is that right? Is that your writing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, this isn't my writing, my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The other suggestion is that it is a network of mines and explosives. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is right that they were positioned, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I didn't say it was the witness's handwriting. When I said "yours," I meant theirs, not his personally. Their document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be allowed to give an explanation of this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I know the terrain very well, and I know what happened there. In Vitaljina, for example, we had a police patrol there, and we didn't go further than Vitaljina with our police forces. We restricted them to that area. From Vitaljina, one kilometre in front of Vitaljina, we placed the mines and explosive devices which were never activated. We never activated them, even when, as you say, the Yugoslav or People's Army, as you call it, attacked that area of Konavle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether that diagram is correct.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC
